topic: Cloud models, networks and service models

notes.front: What does ‘on-premises’ mean for an organisation’s apps and data?
notes.back: The organisation hosts and manages its own apps and data on servers in its own data centre or facility.
notes.explanation: The study guide sets this model beside private and public cloud as the starting point: everything is owned and run in-house.
notes.example: Like keeping your savings in a safe at home rather than in a bank: a law firm runs its case database on servers in its own basement.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader study guide, “Digital Transformation with Google Cloud”, “Cloud deployment models and strategies”, p. 1
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is a private cloud?
notes.back: Cloud computing resources used by one organisation only.
notes.explanation: What makes it private is exclusive use, not location: the study guide allows the resources to sit on-premises or with a third-party provider.
notes.example: Like a gym inside an office block that only that company’s staff may use: a bank’s cloud platform that no other customer shares.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader study guide, “Digital Transformation with Google Cloud”, “Cloud deployment models and strategies”, p. 1
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is a public cloud?
notes.back: Cloud services that a third-party provider, such as Google Cloud, offers over the public internet, with resources shared by many organisations or users.
notes.explanation: Sharing is the defining difference from a private cloud, whose resources serve one organisation only.
notes.example: Like a public swimming pool run by an operator for everyone: many companies run their apps in the same provider’s data centres.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader study guide, “Digital Transformation with Google Cloud”, “Cloud deployment models and strategies”, p. 1
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In Google’s architecture guidance, what is hybrid cloud?
notes.back: An architecture that deploys workloads across a public cloud and at least one private environment, such as an on-premises data centre.
notes.explanation: Google’s guide names a colocation facility as another example of the private side.
notes.example: Like a shop that keeps its own stockroom but rents extra space at a shared depot for busy seasons: a retailer keeps its order database in its data centre and runs its website on Google Cloud.
notes.source: Google Cloud Architecture Center, “Build hybrid and multicloud architectures using Google Cloud”, “Overview of hybrid cloud and multicloud”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: the term hybrid cloud describes an architecture in which workloads are deployed across multiple computing environments, one based in the public cloud, and at least one being private—for example, an on-premises data center or a colocation facility.

notes.front: In Google’s architecture guidance, what is multicloud?
notes.back: An architecture that combines at least two public cloud providers.
notes.explanation: The providers must both be public; Google adds that such an architecture sometimes also includes a private computing environment.
notes.example: Like a household that banks with two different banks: a media company processes video on Google Cloud and runs billing on another public provider.
notes.source: Google Cloud Architecture Center, “Build hybrid and multicloud architectures using Google Cloud”, “Overview of hybrid cloud and multicloud”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: The term multicloud describes an architecture that combines at least two public CSPs. As illustrated in the following diagram, sometimes this architecture includes a private computing environment

notes.front: What is an IP address?
notes.back: A unique numerical label that acts as a device’s digital mailing address on a network.
notes.explanation: The study guide’s networking terms start here: the Domain Name System exists to turn names into these numbers.
notes.example: Like the house number on a street: a web server might be found at 203.0.113.10.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader study guide, “Digital Transformation with Google Cloud”, “Networking terms and concepts”, p. 2
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What does the Domain Name System (DNS) do?
notes.back: It translates human-readable web addresses into numerical IP addresses.
notes.explanation: People remember names and networks route by numbers, and the study guide defines the Domain Name System as the translator between the two.
notes.example: Like the contacts list on a phone: you tap a name and the phone dials the number; you type example.com and DNS supplies the server’s IP address.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader study guide, “Digital Transformation with Google Cloud”, “Networking terms and concepts”, p. 2
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is Cloud DNS?
notes.back: Google Cloud’s Domain Name System service, which publishes your domain names to the global DNS.
notes.explanation: Google describes it as high-performance, resilient and global, and says it does the publishing cost-effectively.
notes.example: Like a directory publisher that lists your shop’s name and number in the national phone book for you: a firm uses it to make shop.example.com resolve worldwide.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Cloud DNS overview”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: Cloud DNS is a high-performance, resilient, global Domain Name System (DNS) service that publishes your domain names to the global DNS in a cost-effective way.

notes.front: In networking, what is latency?
notes.back: The time a data packet takes to travel from its source to its destination.
notes.explanation: It is a measure of time, which the study guide keeps separate from bandwidth, a measure of how much data fits through a connection.
notes.example: Like the delay between posting a letter and its arrival: a request from London to a server in Sydney takes longer to arrive than one to a server in Paris.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader study guide, “Digital Transformation with Google Cloud”, “Networking terms and concepts”, p. 2
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In networking, what is bandwidth?
notes.back: The maximum amount of data that can be transmitted over a network connection in a given amount of time.
notes.explanation: It is a capacity, an upper limit on volume per unit of time, rather than a travel time.
notes.example: Like the number of lanes on a motorway: more lanes let more cars through each hour.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader study guide, “Digital Transformation with Google Cloud”, “Networking terms and concepts”, p. 2
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In Google Cloud, what is a region?
notes.back: An independent geographic area that consists of zones.
notes.explanation: Regions and zones are logical abstractions over the underlying physical resources, such as data centres.
notes.example: Like a city made up of several districts: Google Cloud’s Osaka region is one such area, with its own zones.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Geography and regions”, “Regions and zones”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: Regions are independent geographic areas that consist of zones. Zones and regions are logical abstractions of underlying physical resources.

notes.front: In Google Cloud, what is a zone?
notes.back: A deployment area for Google Cloud resources within a region.
notes.explanation: Google says to treat each zone as a single failure domain within its region.
notes.example: Like one district of a city: a region holds several zones, each a separate place to deploy resources.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Geography and regions”, “Regions and zones”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: A zone is a deployment area for Google Cloud resources within a region. Zones should be considered a single failure domain within a region.

notes.front: In Google Cloud’s network, what is an edge location?
notes.back: One of many globally distributed points of presence that cache content near users.
notes.explanation: The study guide lists edge locations with regions and zones as the parts of Google Cloud’s network; Google’s documentation also calls them points of presence.
notes.example: Like a parcel locker in your street that holds copies of popular items, so you need not wait for the central warehouse.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader study guide, “Digital Transformation with Google Cloud”, “Google Cloud’s network”, p. 2
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is Google’s global network?
notes.back: Google’s purpose-built private fibre network, which handles all Google Cloud customer traffic across the globe.
notes.explanation: The study guide counts it among Google Cloud’s strengths and describes it under the security of Google’s own infrastructure.
notes.example: Like a company’s private motorway between its depots: a customer’s traffic between two continents can stay on Google’s own cables instead of the open road.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader study guide, “Trust and Security with Google Cloud”, “Google-built global network and data centers”, p. 13
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is Cloud CDN (Content Delivery Network)?
notes.back: A Google Cloud service that uses Google’s global edge network to serve content closer to users, speeding up websites and applications.
notes.explanation: It does not work alone: it works with an Application Load Balancer, global external or classic, to deliver content.
notes.example: Like a publisher that stocks a bestseller in every local bookshop instead of posting each copy from its warehouse: a news site’s images are served from caches near readers.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Cloud CDN overview”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: Cloud CDN (Content Delivery Network) uses Google's global edge network to serve content closer to users, which accelerates your websites and applications. Cloud CDN works with the global external Application Load Balancer or the classic Application Load Balancer to deliver content to your users.

notes.front: What is Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS)?
notes.back: A cloud service model that gives on-demand access to core resources, such as compute and storage, without owning the hardware.
notes.explanation: The study guide highlights high scalability and a pay-as-you-go model as its features.
notes.example: Like renting an empty commercial kitchen by the hour: the ovens are there, but you bring the recipes, the cooks and the ingredients.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader study guide, “Digital Transformation with Google Cloud”, “Cloud computing service models”, p. 2
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is Platform as a Service (PaaS)?
notes.back: A cloud service model giving developers a complete environment to build and run applications, while the provider manages patches and infrastructure.
notes.explanation: The customer’s effort moves to writing and running code; the platform underneath is someone else’s job.
notes.example: Like a kitchen whose owners maintain and clean all the equipment: you arrive and cook.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader study guide, “Digital Transformation with Google Cloud”, “Cloud computing service models”, p. 2
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is Software as a Service (SaaS)?
notes.back: A cloud service model that delivers complete, ready-to-use applications through a web browser, with no local installation or maintenance.
notes.explanation: The study guide describes it as a cost-effective solution paid for by subscription.
notes.example: Like eating at a restaurant: you get the finished meal and never set foot in the kitchen.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader study guide, “Digital Transformation with Google Cloud”, “Cloud computing service models”, p. 2
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Where can the resources of a private cloud physically be?
notes.back: On the organisation’s own site, or managed by a third-party provider.
notes.explanation: A private cloud is defined by exclusive use by one organisation, so either location qualifies.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader study guide, “Digital Transformation with Google Cloud”, “Cloud deployment models and strategies”, p. 1
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In a hybrid strategy, what does adding public cloud let an organisation do without up-front capital investment?
notes.back: Extend the capacity and capabilities of its computing platforms.
notes.explanation: Google adds that the organisation also keeps its existing investments and avoids committing itself to a single cloud vendor.
notes.source: Google Cloud Architecture Center, “Build hybrid and multicloud architectures using Google Cloud”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: By using the public cloud, you can extend the capacity and capabilities of your computing platforms without up-front capital investment costs. By adding one or more public cloud based solutions, like Google Cloud, to your existing infrastructure, you not only preserve your existing investments, but you also avoid committing yourself to a single cloud vendor.

notes.front: What does Google’s guide call an architecture that combines at least two public cloud providers and also includes a private computing environment?
notes.back: A hybrid and multicloud architecture.
notes.explanation: Multicloud needs only the public providers; the private environment, which may include a private cloud, is what adds the hybrid part.
notes.source: Google Cloud Architecture Center, “Build hybrid and multicloud architectures using Google Cloud”, “Overview of hybrid cloud and multicloud”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: sometimes this architecture includes a private computing environment (that might include the use of a private cloud component). That arrangement is called a hybrid and multicloud architecture.

notes.front: What is the difference between hybrid cloud and multicloud?
notes.back: Hybrid cloud pairs a public cloud with at least one private environment; multicloud combines at least two public cloud providers.
notes.explanation: The deciding question is whether a private environment is involved (hybrid) or several public providers are (multicloud).
notes.source: Google Cloud Architecture Center, “Build hybrid and multicloud architectures using Google Cloud”, “Overview of hybrid cloud and multicloud”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: one based in the public cloud, and at least one being private—for example, an on-premises data center or a colocation facility. The term multicloud describes an architecture that combines at least two public CSPs.

notes.front: A games studio has no data centre of its own. It runs its multiplayer servers on Google Cloud and its payments system on another public cloud provider. Which architecture is this?
notes.back: C: it combines two public cloud providers.
notes.choices:
A) Hybrid cloud
B) Private cloud
C) Multicloud
D) On-premises
notes.choicesExplained: A: hybrid cloud needs at least one private environment, and the studio has none. B: nothing here is used by one organisation alone. D: the studio runs nothing on its own servers.
notes.explanation: Google defines multicloud as an architecture that combines at least two public cloud providers, which is exactly this set-up.
notes.source: Google Cloud Architecture Center, “Build hybrid and multicloud architectures using Google Cloud”, “Overview of hybrid cloud and multicloud”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: The term multicloud describes an architecture that combines at least two public CSPs.

notes.front: A hospital keeps its patient records system in its own data centre but runs its appointment-booking website on Google Cloud. Which architecture is this?
notes.back: C: one public cloud plus one private environment.
notes.choices:
A) Public cloud only
B) Multicloud
C) Hybrid cloud
D) Software as a Service
notes.choicesExplained: A: part of the estate is in the hospital’s own data centre. B: multicloud needs at least two public cloud providers; there is only one here. D: SaaS is a service model, not a way of combining environments.
notes.explanation: Google’s definition of hybrid cloud is workloads spread across a public cloud and at least one private environment, such as an on-premises data centre.
notes.source: Google Cloud Architecture Center, “Build hybrid and multicloud architectures using Google Cloud”, “Overview of hybrid cloud and multicloud”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: the term hybrid cloud describes an architecture in which workloads are deployed across multiple computing environments, one based in the public cloud, and at least one being private—for example, an on-premises data center or a colocation facility.

notes.front: A small architecture practice runs its file server and accounts software on two machines in its own office, managed by its own staff. Which model is this?
notes.back: C: its own apps and data on its own servers.
notes.choices:
A) Public cloud
B) Multicloud
C) On-premises
D) Platform as a Service
notes.choicesExplained: A: nothing is provided by a third party over the internet. B: no cloud provider is involved at all. D: PaaS is a platform run by a provider, not in-house servers.
notes.explanation: The study guide’s on-premises model is an organisation hosting and managing its own apps and data on servers in its own facility.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader study guide, “Digital Transformation with Google Cloud”, “Cloud deployment models and strategies”, p. 1
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A defence agency has a cloud platform built for it alone; a contractor runs it in the contractor’s own building, and no other customer shares it. Which model is this?
notes.back: C: cloud resources used by one organisation only.
notes.choices:
A) Public cloud
B) Multicloud
C) Private cloud
D) On-premises
notes.choicesExplained: A: public cloud resources are shared by many organisations. B: only one provider is involved. D: the servers are not in the agency’s own facility.
notes.explanation: A private cloud may be run by a third-party provider; exclusive use by one organisation is what makes it private.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader study guide, “Digital Transformation with Google Cloud”, “Cloud deployment models and strategies”, p. 1
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What are two common business drivers Google names for choosing a hybrid architecture?
notes.back: Any two, among others: heeding data sovereignty laws, and reducing capital expenditure or general spending on technology.
notes.explanation: Google’s list is headed ‘some common’ drivers, so it is open; the cost driver is paired with cloud financial management and cost optimisation disciplines.
notes.source: Google Cloud Architecture Center, “Drivers, considerations, strategy, and approaches”, “Business and technical drivers”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: Some common, influencing, business drivers when choosing a hybrid architecture include the following: - Heeding laws and regulations about data sovereignty. - Reducing capital expenditure (CAPEX) or general IT spending with the support of cloud financial management and cost optimization disciplines like FinOps.

notes.front: What are two common challenges of a multicloud strategy, according to Google?
notes.back: Any two, among others: more management complexity, keeping security consistent, and integrating software environments.
notes.explanation: Google warns that such challenges can sometimes outweigh the benefits, and that multicloud may add costs later on.
notes.source: Google Cloud Architecture Center, “Drivers, considerations, strategy, and approaches”, “Business and technical drivers”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: Sometimes, the potential challenges associated with a multicloud strategy might outweigh the benefits. A multicloud strategy might introduce additional costs later on. Common challenges associated with developing a multicloud strategy include the following: - Increasing management complexity. - Maintaining consistent security. - Integrating software environments.

notes.front: In Google Cloud, what do IP addresses let resources such as virtual machines and load balancers do?
notes.back: Communicate with other resources in Google Cloud, in on-premises networks or on the public internet.
notes.explanation: Google’s IP address page groups addresses by where they can be reached from, starting from this purpose.
notes.source: Google Cloud, VPC documentation, “IP addresses”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: These IP addresses let Google Cloud resources communicate with other resources in Google Cloud, in on-premises networks, or on the public internet.

notes.front: What is the difference between an internal and an external IP address in Google Cloud?
notes.back: An external IP address is publicly routed; an internal one is not.
notes.explanation: Public routing is the whole difference, and Google notes you can give an external address to a Google Cloud virtual machine’s network interface.
notes.source: Google Cloud, VPC documentation, “IP addresses”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: For example, an internal IP address is not publicly routed. An external IP address is a publicly routed IP address. You can assign an external IP address to the network interface of a Google Cloud VM.

notes.front: What generally happens to an ephemeral IP address when you stop or delete the resource it belongs to?
notes.back: In general it is released, because an ephemeral address doesn’t persist beyond the life of the resource.
notes.explanation: Its lifetime is tied to the resource it serves, which is what makes it ephemeral.
notes.source: Google Cloud, VPC documentation, “IP addresses”, “Ephemeral and static IP addresses”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: An ephemeral IP address is an IP address that doesn't persist beyond the life of the resource. In general, ephemeral IP addresses are released if you stop or delete the associated resource.

notes.front: A payments firm’s partners only accept traffic from one agreed IP address. The firm will soon replace the server that uses it and must keep the same address. What should it use?
notes.back: D: a static address stays assigned to the project until you release it.
notes.choices:
A) Cloud CDN caching
B) An ephemeral IP address
C) A new Cloud DNS zone
D) A reserved static IP address
notes.choicesExplained: A: caching content does not fix a server’s address. B: an ephemeral address is generally released when its resource is stopped or deleted. C: a DNS zone maps names to addresses; it does not keep the address itself.
notes.explanation: Google says reserving one suits a service that depends on a specific address and must prevent other resources from using it.
notes.source: Google Cloud, VPC documentation, “IP addresses”, “Ephemeral and static IP addresses”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: Reserving a static IP address assigns the address to your project until you explicitly release it. This is useful if you are dependent on a specific IP address for your service and need to prevent another resource from being able to use the address.

notes.front: What kind of database does Google’s Cloud DNS documentation say the Domain Name System is?
notes.back: A hierarchical, distributed database for storing IP addresses and other data and looking them up by name.
notes.explanation: Looking data up by name is what lets a typed web address be turned into a numerical address.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Cloud DNS overview”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: DNS is a hierarchical distributed database that lets you store IP addresses and other data and look them up by name.

notes.front: A customer types a shop’s web address into a browser. Which system turns that name into the numerical address the browser needs to reach the shop’s server?
notes.back: C: DNS translates web addresses into IP addresses.
notes.choices:
A) Bandwidth
B) An edge location
C) The Domain Name System
D) Latency
notes.choicesExplained: A: bandwidth is how much data a connection can carry. B: an edge location caches content near users; it does not translate names. D: latency is a travel time, not a system.
notes.explanation: The study guide defines DNS as the translator from human-readable web addresses to numerical IP addresses.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader study guide, “Digital Transformation with Google Cloud”, “Networking terms and concepts”, p. 2
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What does Cloud DNS spare you when you publish your zones and records?
notes.back: Managing your own DNS servers and software.
notes.explanation: Google adds that Cloud DNS offers private managed zones as well as public ones.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Cloud DNS overview”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: Cloud DNS lets you publish your zones and records in DNS without the burden of managing your own DNS servers and software. Cloud DNS offers both public zones and private managed DNS zones.

notes.front: How does latency differ from bandwidth?
notes.back: Latency is how long a packet takes to travel; bandwidth is how much data a connection can carry in a given time.
notes.explanation: One is a delay and the other a capacity; the study guide defines them as separate terms.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader study guide, “Digital Transformation with Google Cloud”, “Networking terms and concepts”, p. 2
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: On a video call between offices on two continents, each remark is heard about a second after it is spoken, although the connection is carrying very little data. Which property is the problem?
notes.back: C: the delay is the time data takes to travel.
notes.choices:
A) Bandwidth
B) An ephemeral IP address
C) Latency
D) The Domain Name System
notes.choicesExplained: A: the connection is barely used, so its capacity is not the limit. B: an address type does not add a delay to each remark. D: DNS only turns names into addresses before the call connects.
notes.explanation: Latency is the travel time of a packet from source to destination; the barely used connection rules out a capacity limit.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader study guide, “Digital Transformation with Google Cloud”, “Networking terms and concepts”, p. 2
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A firm’s nightly backup of several terabytes to the cloud is still running when staff arrive in the morning, because the office link can carry only a limited amount of data per second. Which property limits it?
notes.back: A: the maximum data a connection carries in a given time.
notes.choices:
A) Bandwidth
B) An edge location
C) Latency
D) A zone
notes.choicesExplained: B: an edge location caches content for users; it does not speed an upload. C: latency is the travel time of each packet, not the volume the link can carry. D: a zone is a deployment area, not a property of the office link.
notes.explanation: Bandwidth caps how much data can pass in a given time, and that cap is what holds back a very large transfer.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader study guide, “Digital Transformation with Google Cloud”, “Networking terms and concepts”, p. 2
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: How many zones does a Google Cloud region normally consist of?
notes.back: Three or more, housed in three or more physical data centres.
notes.explanation: A few regions, such as Stockholm and Osaka, have three zones in only one or two data centres while they expand to at least three.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Geography and regions”, “Regions and zones”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: A region consists of three or more zones housed in three or more physical data centers. The regions Stockholm, Mexico, Osaka, and Montreal have three zones housed in one or two physical data centers. These regions are in the process of expanding to at least three physical data centers.

notes.front: Choosing where to locate your applications among Google Cloud’s regions and zones helps you meet which three kinds of requirement?
notes.back: Latency, availability and durability.
notes.explanation: Locations span North America, South America, Europe, Asia, the Middle East and Australia, divided into regions and zones.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Geography and regions”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: Google Cloud infrastructure services are available in locations across North America, South America, Europe, Asia, the Middle East, and Australia. These locations are divided into regions and zones. You can choose where to locate your applications to meet your latency, availability, and durability requirements.

notes.front: What does Google advise to make applications fault-tolerant and highly available against unexpected failures?
notes.back: Deploy them across multiple zones in a region.
notes.explanation: Google treats each zone as a single failure domain within its region.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Geography and regions”, “Regions and zones”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: Zones should be considered a single failure domain within a region. To deploy fault-tolerant applications with high availability and help protect against unexpected failures, deploy your applications across multiple zones in a region.

notes.front: An online ticket seller runs all its web servers in one Google Cloud zone. It wants the site to stay up if that zone fails. What should it do?
notes.back: C: spread the application across several zones in the region.
notes.choices:
A) Switch every server to an ephemeral IP address
B) Move all the servers to a larger machine in the same zone
C) Deploy the servers across multiple zones in the region
D) Add more bandwidth to the office network
notes.choicesExplained: A: the address type does not protect against a zone failure. B: one zone is still a single failure domain, however large the machine. D: office bandwidth has nothing to do with the zone’s availability.
notes.explanation: Google treats a zone as a single failure domain and advises deploying across multiple zones for fault tolerance and high availability.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Geography and regions”, “Regions and zones”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: Zones should be considered a single failure domain within a region. To deploy fault-tolerant applications with high availability and help protect against unexpected failures, deploy your applications across multiple zones in a region.

notes.front: An insurer keeps its claims data in regional storage in one Google Cloud region. It must be able to recover if that whole region is lost. What does Google strongly recommend?
notes.back: D: copy the data out of the region for disaster recovery.
notes.choices:
A) Adding more zones inside the same region
B) Moving the data to an edge location
C) Switching to a new Cloud DNS zone
D) Replicating the data to another region or snapshotting it to multi-regional storage
notes.choicesExplained: A: extra zones in the same region are lost with the region. B: edge locations cache content for users; they are not a store for claims data. C: a DNS zone holds name records, not the data itself.
notes.explanation: For regional or zonal storage, Google strongly recommends replicating to another region or snapshotting to a multi-regional resource for disaster recovery.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Geography and regions”, “Geographic management of data”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: When using regional or zonal storage resources, we strongly recommend that you replicate data to another region or snapshot it to a multi-regional storage resource for disaster recovery purposes.

notes.front: Google manages some services to be redundant within and across regions. What trade-off do these multi-regional services require?
notes.back: A trade-off between latency and the consistency model.
notes.explanation: Spreading them across regions optimises availability, performance and resource efficiency, and that is what creates the trade-off.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Geography and regions”, “Multi-regional resources”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: Multiple Google Cloud services are managed by Google to be redundant and distributed within and across regions. These services optimize availability, performance, and resource efficiency. As a result, these services require a trade-off between either latency or the consistency model.

notes.front: What does Google’s global network of peering points of presence let customer traffic do?
notes.back: Travel within the Google network until it is close to its destination.
notes.explanation: Google says this gives users a better experience and better security.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Geography and regions”, “Points of presence (POPs)”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: Google operates a global network of peering points of presence, which means that customer traffic can travel within the Google network until it's close to its destination, providing users with a better experience and better security.

notes.front: A news website hosted in one region has readers on every continent, and its popular photos load slowly for distant readers. Which part of Google Cloud’s network is designed to hold copies of such content near those readers?
notes.back: A: points of presence that cache content near users.
notes.choices:
A) Edge locations
B) A reserved static IP address
C) A second zone in the same region

notes.choicesExplained: B: a fixed address does not move content closer. C: another zone sits in the same region, no nearer the distant readers. D: a private cloud is a deployment model, not a way to cache content worldwide.

notes.front: According to the study guide, what does carrying customer traffic on Google’s own global network reduce?
notes.back: Exposure to the public internet.
notes.explanation: The guide adds that it enables fast, secure communication around the world.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader study guide, “Trust and Security with Google Cloud”, “Google-built global network and data centers”, p. 13

notes.front: How does Google’s global backbone reduce end-user latency?
notes.back: By having interconnects close to users.
notes.explanation: Google adds that the same backbone gives great flexibility for load balancing.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Geography and regions”, “Global services”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: Our global backbone provides tremendous flexibility for load-balancing, and reduces end-user latency by having interconnects close to you.

notes.front: A bank wants its customers’ traffic to stay off the public internet for as much of its journey as possible. Which Google Cloud strength addresses this?
notes.back: B: traffic travels on Google’s own network until it is close to its destination.
notes.choices:
A) Integration tax
B) Google’s global network
C) An ephemeral IP address
D) Software as a Service
notes.choicesExplained: A: integration tax is a driver of transformation, not a network. C: an address type does not change the route traffic takes. D: SaaS is a service model, not a network.
notes.explanation: Google’s peering points of presence let customer traffic stay within the Google network until it nears its destination, which Google says improves security.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Geography and regions”, “Points of presence (POPs)”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: customer traffic can travel within the Google network until it's close to its destination, providing users with a better experience and better security.

notes.front: In Cloud CDN, what is a cache hit?
notes.back: A request answered with a cached copy of the content, found in the Cloud CDN cache.
notes.explanation: Answering from cache shortens the round-trip time and saves the origin server from having to process the request.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Cloud CDN overview”, “Cache hits and cache misses”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: finds a cached response to the user's request, the GFE sends the cached response to the user. This is called a cache hit. When a cache hit occurs, the GFE looks up the content by its cache key and responds directly to the user, shortening the round-trip time and saving the origin server from having to process the request.

notes.front: When popular cacheable requests are served from a Cloud CDN cache, which three benefits does Google say you can expect?
notes.back: Significantly reduced latency, reduced cost and reduced load on your origin servers.
notes.explanation: Google cannot predict whether any one request is served from a cache, but expects popular cacheable content to be, most of the time.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Cloud CDN overview”, “Serve content from a cache”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: it is impossible to predict whether a particular request is served out of a cache. You can, however, expect that popular requests for cacheable content are served from a cache most of the time, yielding significantly reduced latencies, reduced cost, and reduced load on your origin servers.

notes.front: Under IaaS, what stays the customer’s responsibility?
notes.back: The operating system, middleware, virtual machines, and any apps and data.
notes.explanation: The provider looks after the data centre infrastructure, so the customer no longer manages, maintains or updates it.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “PaaS vs. IaaS vs. SaaS vs. CaaS: How are they different?”, “IaaS”

notes.front: Under PaaS, what does the customer still do, and what does the provider handle?
notes.back: The customer writes code and manages its data and apps; the provider manages the servers and scaling.
notes.explanation: Google’s comparison says customers bring their own code and deploy it, while the build and run environment is the provider’s to maintain.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “PaaS vs. IaaS vs. SaaS vs. CaaS: How are they different?”, “Key differences between cloud IaaS, PaaS, SaaS, and CaaS”

notes.front: Under SaaS, what is the customer still responsible for?

notes.explanation: The provider manages, maintains and secures the application itself, including updates and bug fixes.

notes.front: A company rents virtual machines from a cloud provider, then installs and patches its own operating system and database on them. Which service model is this?
notes.back: D: IaaS: rented infrastructure, with the operating system and above left to the customer.
notes.choices:
A) On-premises
B) Platform as a Service
C) Software as a Service
D) Infrastructure as a Service
notes.choicesExplained: A: the machines are rented from a provider, not owned in-house. B: under PaaS the provider would run the platform and the customer would just deploy code. C: under SaaS the customer would use a finished application.
notes.explanation: With IaaS the customer is responsible for the operating system, middleware, virtual machines, apps and data.

A) Infrastructure as a Service

notes.front: Of IaaS, PaaS and SaaS, which gives the highest level of control over infrastructure, and what is the cost of that control?
notes.back: IaaS; the customer must handle hands-on configuration and maintenance, and its own data security and recovery.
notes.explanation: Google’s comparison puts control and responsibility on the same scale: PaaS and SaaS hand more to the provider and leave less control.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “PaaS vs. IaaS vs. SaaS vs. CaaS: How are they different?”, “Choosing which is right for you: pros and cons”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What does Google’s comparison list as SaaS’s main advantages and disadvantages?
notes.back: Easy to set up and fully managed by the provider, but no control over infrastructure or security controls and little to no customisation.
notes.explanation: It sits at the opposite end from IaaS: the most is handed to the provider, and the least control is left with the customer.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “PaaS vs. IaaS vs. SaaS vs. CaaS: How are they different?”, “Choosing which is right for you: pros and cons”
